name: Aisha Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am a construction worker on building sites, mostly setting timber partitions and fitting roof pieces before the coverings go on. I have a vocational trade certificate and plenty of ordinary site experience; I am no supervisor. I use AI every day to sort delivery notes and sketch a cutting order, then check every length against the timber in front of me. My husband Pavel and I have two school-age children, a mortgage, higher pay for this trade and more than nine months of expenses saved. Plenty of contractors work nearby, though a good site crew is worth keeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the site team that a little paperwork saved is welcome if the timber count remains honest. I already use AI for delivery notes, and I check the stack before anybody starts cutting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our wages and mortgage plan look safe in this picture. I enjoy a useful tool. A neat timber list can still hide one missing beam that stops a roof crew at lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my partition and roof-fitting shifts and use the same delivery-note tool. In the first year I would add a photo of each timber bundle before the AI list is sent to the foreman.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I would rather use the ten saved minutes to get the roof closed before rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the photo prove?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bundle label and the actual number of pieces can be checked together. If the list says twelve and the stack holds eleven, the foreman can order one before the lift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy the tool yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The contractor provides it, and I would not spend family money to make a delivery note prettier.

say: **AI delivery notes** help when the timber count is checked at the stack.
**Physical fitting** still depends on the pieces that arrived.
think: Our **wages and mortgage plan** look secure.
A missing **roof beam** can stop a crew despite a tidy list.
do: **Keep** partition and roof-fitting shifts with existing AI notes.
**Attach** bundle photos before sending timber lists to the foreman.
feel: **Calm**, with an eye on finishing before rain.
S0.quote: A neat timber list can still hide one missing beam that stops a roof crew at lunch.
fieldNote: She uses **AI daily** for delivery notes and cutting orders while still counting the actual timber on site.
Her **higher pay and savings** make a small paperwork change financially easy.

steps.text: Keep partition and roof-fitting shifts with existing AI notes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AI could make buying and schedules more accurate before robots are common on site. I would test the new delivery plan on actual roof jobs rather than accept a promise of perfect timing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A quicker order might help, but an office that cuts buyers could leave me chasing the wrong timber. I expect my own pay to hold given our strong buffer and nearby contractors; the apprentice waiting for a missing bundle would feel the waste first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would run the planning tool on four roof jobs and log missing pieces, late deliveries and hours saved. In the first year I would show the result to the site manager and keep the new schedule only where it matched the deliveries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interested, with a bit of unease for the crew if buying staff vanish. I would like a better plan, just one tested against the truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which missing piece matters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A short ridge board can stop the roof covering even if every small batten is there. I would log the lost hours beside the delivery list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if all four jobs arrive correctly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use the plan and tell the manager it earned our trust. I would still make the apprentice count the bundle before anyone lifts it.

say: **Buying and scheduling** change before capable robots can assemble physical roof frames on building sites.
think: My **own pay** looks secure, but a missing bundle could waste apprentice time.
do: **Test** planning AI on four roof jobs and log delivery results.
**Use** the new schedule only where actual deliveries match.
feel: **Interested**, with unease about missing buyers and timber.
S1.quote: A short ridge board can stop the roof covering even if every small batten is there.
fieldNote: She is **quick to trial AI** but keeps a physical bundle count.
Her **income security** shifts attention to apprentices and buying errors, not immediate wage loss.

steps.text: Learn planning AI on four roof jobs using actual delivery logs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my coworkers that thinking AI reaches buying and drawings by 2028, while capable building robots arrive about 2031. We have three years of hands-on site work to find out how the machines handle real timber.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like learning first, but a robot that assembles roofs could take some of my higher-paid shifts after 2031. We have savings and many local contractors, yet the mortgage and school costs mean I will not trade a solid wage for an impressive machine demo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put a fixed hundred from each new pay cheque into savings while our ordinary bills allow it. If the contractor offers paid robot-setup practice on a real trial, I would take it; after 2028 I would apply for a posted local site-setup role only if its wage covers the family bills and any required course is funded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about replacing the wage, but excited to learn. I would rather touch a roof robot’s controls on a safe mock roof than guess from a video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you test on the mock roof?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feed the robot one slightly bowed timber and see whether it flags the piece before fastening anything. The crew should keep a record of any bad cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend your existing savings on training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Pavel and I have saved for household security; the extra hundred from each future pay cheque builds more room, and the employer should fund job-specific training.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes buying before capable roof robots around 2031.
**Real timber trials** should test robot judgment.
think: Robots could reduce **higher-paid roof shifts** after 2031.
Savings and **many contractors** help, but the mortgage still needs a good wage.
do: **Save** one hundred from each new pay cheque if bills allow.
**Take** paid robot-setup practice on a safe trial if offered.
**Apply** after 2028 for posted local setup only with bill-covering pay and funded course.
feel: **Anxious** about pay, keen to learn the controls.
S2.quote: I would rather touch a roof robot’s controls on a safe mock roof than guess from a video.
fieldNote: Her **new saving** comes from future wages, separate from existing household savings.
Her **setup move** requires a posted local vacancy, bill-covering wages and funded training.

steps.text: Save one hundred from each new pay cheque if bills allow
Take paid roof-robot setup practice on safe mock roof if offered
Apply after 2028 for posted local setup only with bill-covering pay and funded course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me test a roof robot through bad weather before thinking AI arrives in 2031. Capable hands-on machines follow about 2034, so I would want an apprentice beside me learning how to stop one safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children will be older and our mortgage may be smaller, but I cannot count on either number today. I might move into site logistics if the work is real and the wage is sound; I would not leave a good roof crew for a job label on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep roof and partition shifts while taking a paid site-logistics course if my employer offers it for a posted local role. In the first year after 2031 I would apply for that role only if the wage covers our household bills; otherwise I would stay on the crew and keep saving one hundred from each new pay cheque when ordinary bills allow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wary, with enough time to try the new job on a real site. A longer runway makes the change less like a leap in the dark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in logistics?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check timber deliveries, safe storage and the order each crew needs materials. I already know how one late roof piece can hold everybody up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge the wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pavel and I would compare it with the mortgage, school and food costs. I would accept a modest drop from today’s higher pay only if we could cover bills without drawing savings each month.

say: **Weather trials** should precede capable site robots around 2034.
**Apprentices** need to learn stop controls beside experienced workers.
think: A **site-logistics role** could fit if the work and wage are real.
The **mortgage and children** still need bill-covering income.
do: **Keep** roof shifts while taking paid logistics course for posted local role.
**Apply** after 2031 only if posted local logistics wage covers bills.
**Save** one hundred from each new pay cheque when ordinary household bills allow.
feel: **Wary**, with time to try a real role.
S3.quote: I would not leave a good roof crew for a job label on a screen.
fieldNote: She defines **logistics duties** through deliveries and storage, not a vague title.
Her **course and application** depend on paid training, a posted local vacancy and bill-covering pay.

steps.text: Take paid site-logistics course if employer offers posted local role
Apply after 2031 for posted local logistics only if wage covers bills
Save one hundred from each new cheque if ordinary bills allow

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade puts thinking AI in 2036 and capable roof-building robots around 2039. I would use the time to pay down the mortgage and teach the children how to count a timber delivery before trusting an app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be in my fifties when robots reach the site, with years of work possibly left. A strong savings cushion cannot replace a construction wage forever. I would like a role that keeps me near real building work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current construction job and put an extra fifty from each pay cheque toward the mortgage if school and food bills allow. In the first year after 2036 I would apply for a posted local materials role only if its wage covers our fixed bills and any required training is paid by the employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly steady, though I still think about those later pay cheques. Ten years lets me cut the debt before I need a different tool belt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the materials role involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would inspect delivered timber and match it to the build order, then tell crews which pieces are missing. I would not take a desk-only title that never sees a site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children work in construction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show them how the trade works and let them choose. I would rather give them measuring skills and a sound budget than promise the same job will wait for them.

say: **2036 thinking AI** arrives before capable building robots can assemble roof frames around 2039.
**Timber counting** remains a useful trade lesson.
think: A **strong savings cushion** cannot replace construction wages for the rest of a working life.
I would prefer **site materials work** to a desk-only title.
do: **Keep** current construction shifts and count physical deliveries.
**Pay** fifty extra toward mortgage from each cheque if bills allow.
**Apply** after 2036 for posted local materials work only with bill-covering pay and funded training.
S4.quote: A strong savings cushion cannot replace a construction wage forever.
fieldNote: Her **extra mortgage payment** comes from future wages only when basic bills allow.
Her **later application** needs a posted local materials role, bill-covering pay and employer-paid training.

steps.text: Keep construction shifts and physical timber checks
Pay fifty extra toward mortgage from each cheque if bills allow
Apply after 2036 for posted local materials only with bill-covering pay and funded training

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because roof-building robots around 2031 could cut well-paid shifts while our children still rely on our wages. Paid setup practice and a posted local role at enough pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what the foreman sees when a robot makes a neat roof frame with one wrong piece. I want the timber count beside the robot report before a crew climbs up.

portrait: **Aisha Novak**, 43, is an experienced construction worker with a vocational trade certificate who fits partitions and roof pieces.
She and husband Pavel have **two school-age children**, a mortgage, higher trade pay and over nine months saved.
She uses **AI daily** for deliveries, tries a roof robot early and saves new wages separately from existing reserves.
In **AGI by 2031**, she considers paid site logistics work only with a posted local vacancy and bill-covering pay.
The **2028 picture** worries her most because robots could cut roof shifts while household costs continue.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut higher-paid roof shifts after 2031 while her children and mortgage still need income.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **robot-setup practice** would let her test a safe mock roof.
A posted local **setup role** at bill-covering pay would protect family income.
headlineQuote: I want the timber count beside the robot report before a crew climbs up.
